content.title: About
content.content: Lima beans are large legumes obtained from the dried seeds of Phaseolus lunatus, a plant native to tropical and subtropical regions. They have a creamy color, a mildly sweet flavor, and a dense, buttery texture when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lima beans are sometimes called “butter beans” because of their smooth texture.
When stored properly, dried beans can keep for 2–3 years.
Ancient cultures in Mexico and the Andes used lima beans in ceremonial dishes.
They are high in starch, making them a popular thickener for soups and stews.
After drying, beans may appear green (young) or yellow (mature).

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked lima beans provides about 15 g of protein, making them a valuable source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of folate (vitamin B9)
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in dried beans and can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lessen its effect.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans may cause bloating in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction to the diet helps.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Raw lima beans contain lectins that are destroyed by cooking; they should never be eaten uncooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried lima beans should be soaked for 6‑8 hours and then boiled for 45‑60 minutes until tender. They can be added to soups, stews, salads, purees, and vegetarian patties. They also make a creamy hummus when blended.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For very long storage (over a year), keep them in the refrigerator or freezer.
